An ellipse is the set of all points in a plane such that the sum of distances to two fixed points, called the foci, is constant. It's the most familiar conic section after the circle, and it appears in planetary orbits, architectural domes, and countless mechanical and optical systems. The standard form is x squared over a squared plus y squared over b squared equals one, where a and b are the semi-major and semi-minor axes. The two foci lie on the major axis at distance c from the center, where c squared equals a squared minus b squared. The eccentricity e equals c over a and measures how stretched the ellipse is. When e equals zero you have a circle. As e approaches one it approaches a parabola. The sum of distances from any point on the ellipse to the two foci is always two a. Kepler discovered that planets orbit the sun in ellipses, not circles, and the sun occupies one focus. Unlike a circle, the perimeter of an ellipse has no closed-form algebraic formula—it requires elliptic integrals. Ellipses have a remarkable reflection property that's exploited in whispering galleries. Sound or light rays from one focus reflect off the elliptical surface directly to the other focus.
